chunks: Limitations of interrupts. The question: What are some limitations of interrupts?
An interrupt lets a peripheral (a hardware block such as a timer or serial port) make the CPU (the processor) pause its work and run a short handler right away.
That is very useful, but it is not free. Interrupts add delay, can be lost, use CPU time, and can corrupt data the main code is using.
Knowing these limits is how you use interrupts safely.
Picture a cook who also answers the doorbell. Every ring stops the cooking.
If a second ring comes before the cook reaches the door, the cook remembers only "someone rang", not how many times. If the bell rings every few seconds, no cooking gets done.
A real CPU resumes exactly where it stopped, but data shared with the handler can still be left half updated.
Two events (A and a second event B) arrive close together.
Event B arrives while ISR A is still running, but the flag is already set, so it adds nothing; when ISR A clears the flag with a blanket clear, B's record disappears and B is lost.
The practical consequences are missed counts, dropped bytes and wrong timestamps unless hardware buffers the events.
Interrupt: ("What interrupts are"): a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause the main code and run a handler.
ISR: ("What an ISR is"): the short handler function that runs in response. Latency: the delay between the event and the first handler instruction.
Jitter: how much that latency changes from one event to the next. Pending flag: one bit that records "an event happened". It cannot count events.
Race condition: a bug where the result depends on whether the interrupt lands before or after a step of the main code.
A sensor sends events at least 100 microseconds apart. The handler takes 8 microseconds. The main code sometimes switches interrupts off for 12 microseconds.
Worst case, an event waits 12 microseconds and then the handler runs 8 microseconds: 20 microseconds in total, well under 100 microseconds, so nothing is lost.
Now switch interrupts off for 150 microseconds instead. A second event arrives while the first is still pending, and the two merge into one. That is the whole idea.
"The main limits are latency and jitter, since masked sections and higher-priority ISRs delay response, so worst case matters.
Events can be lost because there's only one pending bit and a long ISR misses the next event.
Entry and exit overhead makes very high rates infeasible, so those need DMA or timer hardware.
Shared data between ISR and main creates race conditions, nesting uses stack, and ISRs can't block or do heavy work.
I mitigate with short ISRs, deferred processing, careful priorities and hardware offload."
